- from Bell's Weekly Messenger London, December 28, 1843. INTERESTING ANTIQUARIAN DIS- COVERT. On the ldth current, the excavators on the Caledonian Railway, working in the Avon valley, discovered a few miles above Beattook some highly interesting relics of antiquity, coeval with the period when Britain was tinder the sway of all conquering Rome. The first object which attracted attention was the remains of what appeared to have been the foundation of a house. Some copper coins were next turned up, about the size of our halfpennies! on one side there is a male head, probably of one of the emperors, and on the obverse þÿ Caesar þÿRoma;, in Roman characters very similar to those now in use. A sword was next discovered, which appears to be formed of brass. By far the most interesting discovery, however, was that of a small stone trough, inverted, and placed upon a flat block of the same material, which upon examination was found to contain a brazen or bronze case, round in its form, two feet in length, and six inches in diameter. Within this case was a precious manuscript, which at the time it was so carefully concealed must have been of high value in the eyes of its possessor. The manuscript, or rather book, is written on vellum, in rolls, as was the Roman custom, and each roll is connected with the other bv a slip of the same material. In length it is altogether about SO feet, and two in breadth. The writing is beautifully executed in the Latin language, and at the top the words þÿ liistoria IB nine," in large characters, are quite distinct, A

small manuscript was also found in the case, also written on parchment, and about a foot square in size, but the writing ot this is very illegible; on the hack are the words Ad Agricolam," the name of the Governor of Britain under the Emperors Vespasian Titus, and Domitian. These interesting relics, w hich, probably, owe their good preservation to the close manner in which their case w as settled up, have been, in the meantime, carefully taken to Moffat Manse, and the Society of .Antiquarians has been informed of the discovery. It is an historical fact that the Romans entered Scotland ttv Annandale, and distinct evidence of their presence may be seen atlLunswark and other places in the Vale of Annan. Some years ago a copper cooking vessel, apparently of Roman workmanship, was found a few miles below Moffat. þÿ Dumfries Courier .

The Cruelties of Heathenism. þÿ The following extinct of a letter just received from the Rev. J Clark, Baptist missionary on the western coast ot Africa, (utnishes a melancholy illustration of the truth thu' " the daik places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty": þÿ " At Calabar there has been a fearful .sacrifice of more than 100 persons for a son of the late king. 1 be poor creature had been dancing egbo alt the day, and drinking mimby, or palm wine, in large quantities, when lie died the same night It is supposed lie was poisoned- This may be the ease, or it may not ; we cannot tell. þÿ The aged mother cried out in African fienzy that she had lost her last child, and now had none to whom to leave her property; and therefore plenty of slaves must be sacrificed. Those at market, and all who heard in time, fled into the hush, and will remain concealed, or out of the way, until the sacrifices cease, whie.ii is sometimes more than a whole year. The aged mother spoke not in vain ; many were the willing slaves to execute her will The sacrifice took place, nor was it bloodless. Three holes were dug in a house. The corpse was put into the first, with a number of young women ! Into the second slaves were put : and into the third the slaughtered Creoles or town born people. þÿ The proportion (or each hole was stated as follows: þÿ Thirty female slaves, forty male slaves, and twenty nine Creoles. Much was done by Mr. Waddcll and Mr. Edgerly, of the Scotch mission, aridity Captain Milbourne,
of the Dove, in the service of the Baptist mission, to try to persuade King Eyarnba to prevent the sacrifice : but it could not be effected."

The Southern mail has arrived, and we have the New Orleans Picavtine of the 3d inst., from which we select the following in lot mation : þÿ The above journal gives in detail the discussion in the Mexican Congress on therojrl to raise fifteen millions by mortgages on the property of the clergy selling the same if necessary to raise that sum. The pri.jgt was laid before the Mexican Congress on the night of the 7th of January, and on the morning of the 8th the discussion w as commenced, but was limited to 5 þÿo clock in the afternoon, when there was a recess

until 7 in the evening. A stair nrnt was then read from the Vicat General in opposition to the projet. After much discussion, the projet to mortgage the property was carþÿried 55 to 31. The question on giving power to sell the church property was then discussed, and decided in the affirmative þÿ 44 to 35. The ministers agreed that unless means were placed at the command of the Government, the Vice President, could not be responsible for the safety of the country, and they were apprehensive that without funds the army would be disbanded, and would march upon the capital to light the fires of civil war. 1 here wrere no accounts in the Mexican papers received of Congress having taken any action to secure peace with the United States. On the contrary, all the debates contained the most hostile feeling to the Americans. The committee appointed to proceed to San Luis þÿt olosi to inform Santa Anna of his election to the Presidency, state that in ieply to questions relating to the condition of the army, he boasted of having sufficient private means to carry on the war for six months þÿ 1 fie committee left him, highly gratified with the information. The Mexican government has promoted Gen. I, a Vega from the brevet title to the rank of Brigadier General. The Governors of Zacatecas and Durango, hostile to Santa Anna, refuse to comply with his demands to place the ordinary and extraordinary resources of those States at ins disposal. I he Mexican editors appear to be wejl

acquainted with the movements and number of our troops, which they give with great exactness. They published Santa þÿAnna s dispatches of the late attack on Capt. May. J.etters from correspondents mention the rumor of the death of Santa Anna ; but still confirmation is wanted.

In another part of our paper our readers will find a few extracts from the Irish papers, detailing some of the terrible and afflicting scenes which are presented in almost every part of poor Ireland. The heait almost instinctively recoils from contemplating a calamity which has had no parallel within the recollection of any living being. The contents of the provincial journa's received in town this morning ate, if possible more gloomy and alarming than any previously published. The deaths by starvation in the parish of Skull, in the county Cotk, have, it is said, averaged for the past week twenty fioeaday\ In a single parish, 25 a day by ascertained starvation ! ! Hundreds are dying of hunger, diarrhoea, low fever, affections of the chest, and dropsy, brought on by cold and want of food, and fully three fourths of those breathing are reported to be more or less aflected with disease, the conse quencc of the dreadful destitution they are sullering. The report of an agent, sent into the paiixhes of lvilmoe and Cuherah, in the same county, states þÿl otatos they have none þÿ corn food is beyond their reach þÿ the domestic fowl has long since disappeared þÿ the pigs are banished completely the þÿ cows and sheep which were heie and there lo he seen have been disposed of or stolen and þÿeaten (he dogs and cat# have cither died ol hunger, or have bccu
fc»

turned to the use of human beings to meet the dreadful cravings of empty stomachs. The same may be Said of the other parishes i the Cause being the same, the effect is similar. 11 It is of daily occurrence to see the mother Carrying the corpse of her child, or the husband that of his wife, unattended by any other person, to the grave. 1'iiday lust, a young woman Was found drawing tire temains of her lather along the road on a door to lay him in his grave at Abbeystowry. þÿ In a Conversation 1 bad with the manager t)F the National Bank in this town he mentioned he had a large quantity of specie in his coffers, and 1 asked him was that piudenl under present circumstances. His reply Was j had some fears two or three months ago, when the people were robust ami energetic, but now 1 have none. They are physicali,y beau. They are so paralysed and so dejected, that you never see two of them together. Their bodies are so emaciated, their spirits so broken, their intellects so weakened, that neither father nor son converse together, but, with an idiotic gaze, view each þÿother s skeleton forms Under these circumstances thete is no conspiracy; there can be none, and therefore 1 am quite at ease in respect to the safely oi the piopeity in my c urp It is declared by those who have the means of best judging, that one half the population of these baronies will be in their graves before April next: while any person lot lunate enough to have reserved a little means are making preparations to emigrate by t lie

spring ships. All through this counliy ugticulture is completely neglected þÿ Such ts the frightful summary of one day's intelligence from the southern districts of the county ofOo'k. Let us next turn to the Kerry papers The Examiner says þÿ þÿ it is now almost a moekerv of the frightfully appalling destitution which exists in this county to be pat ticularising and cbtouiding a few instances of death from starvation, when numbers are daily dying Irotn this cause, unnoticed and unheard þÿol. In addition to the accounts of several deaths from starvation, the Kerry Examiner contains reports of two serious outbreaks in that county, connected with the want of loud. In the county Mayo ihere Were five inquests hold within three or four days on persons who died suddenly þÿ that is, without any apparent illness; but private letters state that in the neighbourhood of Ballinn, at Balia Foxford, and Crossmolina, the people are dung in scores every day of diseases brought on by want of food, and in many cases by eating raw vegetables. As in the ease of the south of Gork, it is therefore impossible to estimate the daily loss of life in the poor county of Mayo, There are, however, some bright spots in this dark picture. At Newport, the scene of Sir II. O'Jhinel's operations, the people are at least free fiom the pangs of hunger, and otherwise, comparatively speaking, well off'. The double mountain Howitzer will be placed on mules and carried to the naiuial biidge, when the load to the west of the puss will be completely commanded to the distance of 1200 yards, so that the enemy's forces must retire on the approach <4 our columns to ihat distance. Our troops will thus be enabled to move through the pass ai d debouch into an open tableau of land of some miles in extent, without hindiaiiee by the Mexican artillery. Ournnm w ill then make a llank movement on A/tun, which will compel the Mexicans to move on to I exano, 51) miles from Mexico. In the mean time Gen. Scott will trove rapidly on Macoui, Cleeo and the Real del Monte, and thence to Paohuca and Otumba. The road from U.umba to Tezano is exceedingly difficult, and perhaps it may not be necessary to follow it in order to form a junction with our columns at Tezano ; if so, Gen. We Imd that there is hut one opinion amongst all classes on the speech ol Lord Joint Bussell on Monday last. It was said ot one ot the Roman emperors, that from the simplicity amt modesty of his life from youth to mature manhood, no one would have deemed him equal to empire, unless he had afterwards seen turn in the actual exercise of it. We will not quite sav this of Lord John Hussell, as liom his earliest years he has exhibited a degree ot talent, tact and acquired knowledge, which, if not impaired by hereditary VV big principles tied pi opensities, would have pointed him out to ihe eves of all men as eminently adapted to become the Premier ot a nation whose characteristic qualities he so largely represents. We never see him, but we see, as m a mirror, the tiue picture of the English gentleman; that candour of mind, that directness of purpose, that transparent sincerity, that consistency of words and meaning, and that total absence of all equivocation and needless loopholes and reserves, which we are accustomed daily and hourly to see m I tie country gentlemen around us. We only gratify our own feelings when we render him tins justice. It is true that, as a Whig minister, we are directly opposed to the leading principles of his administration, lint non oblusa mien geslamus pec tor n. Truer i, þÿ we were not born in a zone so far from the sun. we are not so fro-

zen in l fie inconge ilia I region of party, as to withhold, even from an adversary, that just recognition ot his fine qualities, which it is the common interest as well as the common duty of all of us to pay, in order to uphold great public merits and to spread and diffuse their example. In conclusion on tins point, we can only say, and we say it heartily. Tails cum sis, utinarn ut nosier esses., lint we must at once enter upon the subject before us, as it is of a complication and importance which require us to dispense with all funher introductory words. The new ministerial plan for Irish relief comprehends the following nine heads or new measures, of which the four first are temporary, and the remaining five permanent. Each of them is to he effected hy a respective hill, and, therefore, both as regards present brevity and the facility of future refetenee, they will be best enumerated hy the specific names of such hills. They are as follows: þÿ I. A bill for the immediate cessation of the present public works after the termination of those of them which, being now in progress, it may tie deemed useful to conclude, 2. A hill to empower government to lend money to a given amount to landed proprietors at threeand a half percent, and for twenty two years, such loan to be used hy them, under the superintendence of government agents, in the employment of labour on their respective estates 3. A bill for the temporary relief of the poor discharged from public works hy food (and not money), hut for a special lime
only; the ultimate limit of such lime to be till the commencement of next harvest, but further to he subject to he shortened at the discretion of the commissioners and board of

guardians, and in all cases to he applied under the workhouse test ; that is, such fo d to be given only to persons who would he teken into the house, or who are in circumstances in which the workhouses would ordinarily give such relief ; the cost to he paid, ore half by local rates and the other half bv government; the administration of such relief to he also under the superintendence of govi iment officers locally attached to eac: depot 4. A bill for the loan of 50 000/. to huidlo us in aid of the purchase of seed for the ensuing harvest, such advance to he spcuied on the crop. The above measures are the tentpotarv acts. Si. A bill for the reclamation of waste lands, to empower government to purchase such lands at their present value ; to reclaim them and render them lit for culma tion from public funds, and nflerwaids to sell or let them in small allotments, from twenty to fifty acres each- 6 A trill for empower ing gooernment to advance money for the extension and improvement ol lush fishetiis, for the purchase of boats, nets, and implements for curing, &c. 7 A full to supply funds to Irish emigrants who shall ha'e arrived at any port in the British American colonies, for the purpose of aiding them to procure work or to make settlements. 8 A bill to empower landowners to mortgage or sell portions of entailed estates, in order to refund government advances and loans, and to convert into freeholds leaseholds now held on lands renewable forever. 9. A hill to enlarge the provisions of the present Irish

poor law. so as to empower hoards of guardians or the commissioners to relieve the aged, sick, and permanently disabled, out of the house (if they deem lit), and to relieve the able bodied poor in the same manner with food, out of the house, when the workhouses are full.

Such are the series and total compass of the plan and new measures now proposed þÿ In our observations upon the respective heads we shall control ourselves with t tint spoil of frankness and patriotism which so obviously influences the whole of the Con>icrvame party, of which we ore members, þÿ sinking at once all selfish and party feelings, and come what may, doing our duty to the distressed Irish, and considering the public good »a paramount to every party and individual object.

Free-trade in Corn. þÿ In the House of Commons, on Friday, Mr. Baillie railed attention to the fact that France and Belgium had prohibited the exportation of corn, and that agents from those countries were making large purchases in the English markets, thus enhancing the price of grain and threatening a scarcity in this country. Under these circumstances he wished to know whether ministers intended to interfere, and profit hit the exportation of corn. Lord John Russell replied on the instant, although no previous notice had been given of the question, that the subject had engaged the attention of himself and his colleagues, and that they had determined not to interfere w ith the usual course of trade, ur.der a full conviction thal, if they were to adopt the suggestion of the hnn. member, they should inflict an injury rather ihan confer a benefit upon the country. If ihe importing merchant leels that he may loing his corn here for consumption, or, if he jreases, take it into another market, he will he induced to tiring his corn here. Hut if he is told that if his corn comes here it will not he allowed to leave the country, he will most likely avoid a muiket, where his corn will be locked np, and go into other markets with his produce.

þÿ M v dear Sir, þÿ Every morning we hear of the deaths of persons to whom no priest had been called, and even some who have been sick for a few days depart this life without the consolations of religion : no clergyman being asked to attend them, so reckless are many of them now become as to their late m this and the life to come. 1 could mention many instances that occurred since my last communication, of the clergymen here meeting with the bodies of the dead ou the same bed or litter with the dying they were called on to attend 'ihere are at this moment persons dead here for days, no one being willing to convey theii ternains to the churchvaid. 1 gave directions to have the bodies of a mother, daughter, and grand daughter buried on Monday last in a keel, wheieonly stillborn children wete buried. They were dead for eight days previous. The deplorable state of the poor baffles every attempt at description. A month back one would believe their condition could not he worse; nevertheless, it is becoming so every moment. They ate reduced to a state ol rabid madness, and epually disregard the laws ol God and man. II one tie sent for flour or bread for the family, he cannot calculate on brmgiug it safely home, as the messengers ate now frequently way laid on the road and depiived of every species of food. I will mention a horrifying circumstance that occurred here on last Thursday evening, and fear we will yet have to record many such frightful facts A man named Donoghue died of starvation son e ten or

twelve days back at Conan, leaving a widow and three children. The poor widow had in a box a small piece of bread and not more than half a stone of flour for them. On Thursday the mother and eldest cliilu left the house, and the two other children in charge of it, one seven the other four years old. She went to seek a basket of turf, and the child took a vessel to hung home soup þÿ in their absence some person came to the hut (which is not many yards from where nearly 200 men are at work) and not onlv took t lie small piece of bread and triflle of flour he found theie, but horrid to relate (probably being known lo ihe children and fearing they may discover on him), he not only cut their throats but nearly severed their heads from their bodies.

þÿ Our farmers here, for the most part, are now as badly off as the labourers. In many instances they have eaten the seed intended for the ground, and their cattle. As to horses, few farmers will have any soon. They are dying in numbers from want of food- When the farmers and labourers are reduced to the same slate of starvation as, 1 lear, will he the case before many days, and no aid afforded the destiiute people through the Public Works, the worst consequences to society and good order may he anticipated þÿ." Alter three days hard fighting both the city and castle oapitu luted, and are now in the possession of the assailants We make the following extracts from the first number of the American tingle of April 3d, which was published in Vera Cruz, a few days after its occupation by the U. THE acknowledged strength, and almost impregnable condition of this City has been a theme for speculation in both hemispheres since the commencement of our present difficulties with Mexico, and many predicted a result very different to that which has so happily fallen upon our arms. The time for ttlid ddack arrived, hut as it drew near, the feats for the issue seemed to increase, and SUh Continued to he the State of feeling on the pilit of many (Who were not as well acquainted with the American character for firmness as they should have been) almost up to the Very moment of the cessation of hostilities But it was hard to overcome the heroism of the noble Spartans, and perhaps no army in existence possess more of that trait Ilian our little þÿarmy the scorching sun, the furious norther, the sand storms and the incessant fire of shells and balls from the Can. ion of the enemy, whilst the work of pre paration was going forward in the shape of planting batteries, diging trenches and throw jug upbrctist works, seemedonly toinspbeour troops with additional courage þÿ these vexations and drawbacks, together with the con tinned appearance of the enemy's cavalry, sometimes within hailing distance of out outposts (making it necessary to keep skirmishing | nrties constantly in employ) would seem sufficient to dishearten rather than encourage us to prosecute with much vigor, the preparations for the mighty struggle for

victory. In consequence of the absence of vessels containing important arms, &«., and the impatience which such delay naturally created, under a galling fire on the part of the enetrfy the attack was commenced on Monday the 22nd u 1 1 . , with considerably less than half the force in the way of mortars, howitzers, &lc, , intended to lie brought 10 bear upon the invested city. The firing on our part commenced about noon of the day, and was kept up with consideiable briskness (relaxation being had at long intervals only, which was spent repairs in of the works, or the gradual increase of batteries.) until the proposition lor a cessation of hostilities, which was received on Thursday night the 25>h Friday, Saturday, and a part of Sunday were consumed in neguciaiion. þÿ On Monday, tire 29th, as per agreement, the Mex.car. Imecs matched out to a beautilul plain, a short distance north west of the city, where they surrendered to those of the United Slates, previously brought upon the ground to receive them þÿ for particulars of the ceremonies which look place afterwards and much oilier interesting matter, we cannot do better than icfer to he several orders emanating from the com-

A T :t mander in chief, and published in this day's paper. Our partiality for, and admiration of many of the officers who occupied conspicuous positions in the attack, and who were the principal actors in the play, would lead us to particularise, were il possible to do so with justice to all, but the fact that every one, (from the director to the most subordinate) performed his tusk with such unheard-of spirit and courage, forbids the indulgence of that wish: for we feel that we would he doing a wrong which we can never consent to participate in, whilst lire heart of an American throbs in out bosom- Although the musket cleared away the ground for t he batteries, it is to their destructive loice we tire compelled to attribute tlte great result. þÿ What might have been achieved by assault, it is, of course impossible to say, hot certain it is, that gteal loss of life on both sides would have been the lamentable consequence, wheteas vast advantages have been derived b\ us from the measures adopted for lire teduclion ot the city with comparatively little loss, and at the same time without a sacrifice ol honor on the part of the loe, whom we most willingly credit with a valorous resistance YVe icjoice at the capitulation, as much on this account almost as from trie advantage derived by us from it, and hope that however chivnhnits the Mexican people may tie, they will be induced in future to acknowledge the superiority of our people in t tie use ol arms, discipline &e., and endeavour henceforth to cope

with us in some other way Our loss so far as we have been able to leant, by frequent enquiry, numbers 17 killed and 12 wounded, among the Killed we could only obtain the names of Capt. Aiburiis, Capt Vinton, and midshipman Shubrick. Y\7c intend however, to make another effort to obtain a list of the names o! all who gloriously h II, which we will give at the eat best possible period.

The facts of the case, which have been communicated to us by an eye witness, and winch can be authenticated on the best authority, are as follows; þÿ While on the above evening the business of die play was going fotward, and while one of the favouitie actresses of the Adelphi was performing her part þÿ indeed we need not hesi late giving the name (Airs. De Bourgh,) as die whole matter is now kept no secret by the parties interested, a tall handsome man, with a military air, in the pit, was observed to look very uneasy for a lew minutes, to gaze earnestly at the stage as if the lady had engaged Ins fixed attention, rising several times from his seat outing die time, until lie at length apparently sattsfieo himself with his security þÿ when, to the astonishment ot all around, lie exclaimed at the pitch of a stern iiulnary voice, þÿ My wife, by Heaven I my Eliza þÿI Not knowing the cause of this sudden outburst, the spectalots for a time appeared at a loss whether to treat the allair in joke or earnest. Seeing, however, dint

the gentleman was perfectly sober, and quite set ions in his manner of address, their merriment gave way to wonder and cuiiosity, which was in no degree lessened when it was noted that the fair actress who bad been thus pointedly addressed had swooned, and requited to leave the stage- The play, however, went on notwithstanding this, but the occurrence excited the most tnaiked attention. On hearing of the matter, Air. At tiler, the manager at once prone ded to the pl ace where the gendemun sat, in order

- þÿto ascertain the cause of the unlooked for inlerruplioh that had been given to the evening's entertainment, and inquired his mi ailing for the expression he had made use of. I tell you,'' said the gentleman, þÿ that lady is my wife, whom 1 have not seen these 19 years 1 have been abroad, and duting that time have not heard from her ; 1 thought her dead: and can you wonder l was astonished? But " said the stranger, þÿ who are you that þÿinquires? Air. Miller replied that he was lessee of the theatre-- that he had a respect for this lady, who had now been in his coips diplomatique for three years, during which her reputed husband, Air, De Bourgh, had died, and as he felt an interest in the reputation of this lady, as well as for the good name of all the members of the company, he hoped the gentleman would not wantonly make a statement to injure her character. þÿ Married," exclaimed the stranger, þÿ- to another A1 y Eliza married ! But 1 must see her immediately, she is still my wife." Mr. Miller asked the name of the gentleman, who said, ' AJy name is Lewis, Lieutenant Lewis, sir. þÿI ve come direct from Liverpool, after having been on foreign service with my boy, her boy, sir. of the representation, when lie found it at once verified by the actress, who find by this time recovered from her faint And now lor the sequel. Alter loving embraces arid hurried explanations, during which the lieutenant seemed to have lived over again lus fiist ihiee years of marriage, the fuilowit g statement was elucidated, which was highly satisfactory to Air Milter and the oiher patties who had the lot tune to be present at the þÿscene: They had married when young in England þÿ he, at the time, a private soldier, site u rising mem ber of a theatrical company in the town of . She, about eight years after the dcpaiture of the vessel with the regiment, had been positively inhumed that ber husband had been killed in battle, and she was married again. The second husband died
